The dissolution of galactomannans in _type II/III_ deep eutectic solvents: Effect of polysaccharide structure and interaction mechanism

ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Galactomannans Deep eutectic solvents Dissolution mechanism Computational quantum chemistry

# ABSTRACT Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have garnered increasing attention as sustainable solvents for natural polysaccharides. Galactomannans (especially guar and locust bean gums) are abundant natural compounds used in food, medicine, agriculture and daily chemical products, whereas their high molecular weight and randomly distributed non-linear structures remain a huge challenge in solubilization and high value-added utilization. In this study, the dissolution of galactomannans in type II/III DESs was comprehensively investigated using density functional theory (DFT) calculation, experimental results, and molecular dynamics simulation (MD). The results indicated that immense anionic and neutral H-bonds supported by type II DESs (consisting of a quaternary ammonium salt and a metal chloride hydrate) could break and rebuild galactomannan H-bond networks, thereby exhibiting remarkable physical solubilization. A large number of active acid sites in type III DESs (consisting of a quaternary ammonium salt and a hydrogen bond donor) greatly improved solubility and cleaved the glycosidic bond, enabling the recovery of polysaccharides with a target molecular weight. Furthermore, significant correlations between solubility and the structure of galactomannans had been established, which meant that high molecular weight and rich galactose side-chains produced repulsive interactions with DESs, directly hindering dissolution. Overall, this work not only offered a framework for enhancing the dissolution of polysaccharides, but also proposed a promising strategy for development of task specific DESs promoting green chemistry and the use of sustainable bioresources.

## 1. Introduction The application of natural polysaccharides in food, medicine, ma-terials and fuels have become an attractive option over the past few decades to mitigate increasing demands for resources in modern society and the promotion of environmental protection (Schlemmer, Selinger, Hobisch, & Spirk, 2021). Due to their biocompatible and biodegradable properties, polysaccharides have been utilized as building blocks to yield polysaccharide-based hydrogels through physical and/or chemical crosslinking of polysaccharides via a variety of monomers or ions. These polysaccharide-derived hydrogels exhibit peculiar physicochemical properties and excellent mechanical properties due to their unique structures and abundant functional groups. (Manzoor et al., 2022). Additionally, cellulose, starch and gel polysaccharides (e.g.

galactomannans) as structural polysaccharides, are commonly used in biomedical fields including bone tissue engineering, cosmetic, food, antibacterial agents etc (Gopinath et al., 2022; Prajapati et al., 2013). Attentions have been paid by galactomannans which exhibit bio- activities such as reducing calorie intakes, controlling blood glucose, and reducing the risks of heart diseases and colon cancer (Li & Nie, 2016; Singh et al., 2021). Galactomannans possess a linear \u03b2-1,4-linked D-mannose backbone to which D-galactose residues are linked by \u03b1-1,6 glycosidic linkages (Moreira & Filho, 2008). In galactomannan family, the chemical structure for each member varies depending on the ratio of mannose to galactose (M/G). For example, the M/G ratio is approxi- mately 4:1 for locust bean gum (LBG, from Ceratonia siliqua) and 2:1 for guar gum (GG, from Cyamopsis tetragonolobus) (Liu et al., 2020; Niknam, Mousavi, & Kiani, 2022). Due to the degree of galactose substitution, the

fine structure of galactomannans is composed of "smooth" zones (lowly substituted) and "hairy" zones (highly substituted), which leads to a dense intra/inter hydrogen bonds networks (Grisel, Aguni, Renou, & Malhiac, 2015). As a result, it is difficult to dissolve in H2O (highly swollen) and traditional organic solvents (dimethyl sulfoxide, form- amide, etc.) that suffers from volatility and flammability, which makes the task specific functionalization very difficult (Depoorter et al., 2019). Thus, a novel, efficient and green solvent system for the functional proliferation of galactomannan is in urgent demand.

Nowadays, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) with low volatility, high designability and low toxicity are considered to have striking applica- tion potential in the processing of natural polysaccharides (Zdanowicz, Wilpiszewska, & Spychaj, 2018). A large number of studies have shown that DESs can achieve efficient solubilization of polysaccharides compared with traditional solvents due to their green characteristics and adjustable physical and chemical properties (Liu et al., 2023). The application of DESs in polysaccharide extraction has great advantages which increases the extraction rate of polysaccharides compared with traditional solvents (Table S1), as reported in extraction of Lycium bar- barum (1.74-fold higher) and Schisandra chinensis polysaccharides (1.39-fold higher) (Gu, Lin, & Zhao, 2023; Yan et al., 2023). This can be explained by the fact that DESs featured by multiple hydrogen bond sites, which provide the abilities to occur hydrogen bonding interaction between DESs and polysaccharides, thereby achieving the purpose of efficient polysaccharides extraction (Pan et al., 2022; Zheng, Hu, Tu, & Wu, 2023). In addition, the task specific functionalization of natural polysaccharides by DESs is an important way to further its high-value utilization. Recent studies have shown that different types of surface chemical functionalization on the cellulose nanofibrils are obtained by using DESs to swell cellulose fibers and weaken of hydrogen bonding network, which confer to the final material distinct properties (Almeida, Maloney, & Gamelas, 2023). Meantime, our previous studies have also confirmed DES/DMSO binary mixed solvents boosting Se-functionalization by enhanced solubilization of hetero- polysaccharide, which is attributed to the disruption of original hydrogen bond networks of polysaccharide, allowing the DESs within the system to interact more easily with polysaccharides (Sun et al., 2022). As is well-known, polysaccharides possess very high structural specificity, including molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, conformation, etc. However, it is important to note that most studies focus primarily on the application of DESs in the field of polysaccharide processing, with limited research conducted on the correlation of DES components with the structure of polysaccharides and the potential dissolution differences (Guo et al., 2021; Prasad & Sharma, 2019). In addition, some researchers have shown that acidic DESs can cause the degradation of polysaccharides, namely, the breaking of glycosidic bonds and the decrease of molecular weight (Yang et al., 2022). One such example is a study by Tian et al. (Tian et al., 2020), who used ChCl-oxalic acid (ChCl-OA) to treat cellulose. As a result, the acidity in ChCl-OA can provide H protons, thus breaking the glycosidic bond and finally obtaining several oligosaccharides linked by β-1,4-glucosidase bonds. The primary issue, therefore, is the relative lack of research on the structure of recovered polysaccharide after DESs treatment. Increased attention on the importance of this topic should attract a research model that systematically compares the dissolution relation- ship between DESs and recovered polysaccharide structure, to prove the physical or chemical dissolution of polysaccharides by DESs.

As discussed above, DESs have the advantage of designability. Based on this feature, an approach of expanding DESs function is the intro- duction of Lewis acid into the conventional _type II_ DESs to prepare _type_ _III_ DESs, which is considered to have great application potential in the field of biomass processing. Using ChCl/glycerol (1:2) as an example, Xia and co-workers show that this system is unable to cleave ether bond linkages in lignin-carbohydrate complexes due to the absence of active protons and acidic sites. Accordingly, based on an acidic multisite co- ordination theory, the _type III_ DESs are designed. The competition of

anionic H-bonds and unidentate aluminum ligands is synchronized to form supramolecular complexes, allowing the multisite bridging ligands to cleave both the H-bonds and ether bonds in lignin-carbohydrate complexes, and the purity of extracted lignin is as high as 94 % (Xia et al., 2018). Additionally, high viscosity is one of the main obstacles to the further application of DESs. The addition of aprotic solvent as the third component to type II DESs can effectively reduce the viscosity of conventional DESs for the further processing and utilization of polysaccharides. For example, the addition of DMSO as a cosolvent to traditional type II DESs can reduce the viscosity and increase the reactivity, which greatly improves the effective conversion of sugar bagasse into platform chemicals (Amesho et al., 2022). Almost simultaneously, it is reported that the conversion rate of hexose in corn stover was significantly increased from 10.95% to 41.40% by using DMSO to reduce the viscosity of ChCl:oxalic acid (Lu et al., 2022). However, given the immense number of HBAs and HBDs, finding "optimal" eutectic mixtures for a given application will currently exhaustive trial-and-error through millions of possible binary combinations (Hansen et al., 2020). This is one of the reasons why the current type III DESs are mostly limited to the treatment of cellulose, and the application of other polysaccharides is less. Moreover, on the one hand, the type III DESs by introducing Lewis acid will form strong anions (OH…Cl) and neutral hydrogen bonds (OH…O), which will break the glycosidic bond of polysaccharides (Ji, Yu, Wu, et al., 2021; Zhou, Fakayode, Yagoub, Ji, & Zhou, 2022); on the other hand, it responds to the molecular weight, branching degree and crystallinity of complex polysaccharides, resulting in different dissolution results. While type III DESs have demonstrated excellent properties in extracting cellulose from biomass, research on type III DESs is still in its early stages (Bai, Zhang, Wang, Zheng, & Yao, 2022; Zhang, Wu, Wang, Li, & Fang, 2024). Particularly, reports on the potential solubilization ability of type III DES in polysaccharides treatment, are rare. Moreover, the influence of type III DESs composition and proportion on the structure of the recovered polysaccharide are not well elucidated, which hinder the development of DESs and their utilization in polysaccharides dissolution and functionalization.

As such, a primary objective of current research is to comparatively evaluate the dissolution relationship between polysaccharide structures and DES components, and to adapt DESs for specific applications. In this work, two typical galactomannans (LBG and GG), with same linear ẞ-1,4-linked D-mannose backbone but different M/G and molecular weight, were employed to study the effect of molecular weight and distribution pattern of Gal substituents on DESs dissolution. First, density functional theory (DFT) calculation was performed to predict the dissolution effects of GG and LBG fragment models in several traditional type II DESs. After preparing and characterizing a series of type II DESs, the optimal type II DES was screened from viscosity, polarity and solubility to LBG and GG. Subsequently, the dissolution mechanism of type II DESs on galactomannans was elucidated by DFT, molecular dynamics simulation (MD) and structural characterization of recovered polysaccharides. Taking advantage of DESs designability, type III DESs with AlCl3-6H2O as the third component were employed to achieve efficient dissolution of galactomannans. The effect of type III DESs with Lewis acid on the structure of the galactomannans during the solubilization was further evaluated by structural characterization of recovered galactomannans. This study aimed to explore the dissolution relationship between polysaccharides structure and DES components, to provide reference for the realization of DESs task specific functionalization and to fully utilize polysaccharide resources.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Choline chloride (ChCl), ethylene glycol (EG), urea, 1,4-butanediol (BDO), glycerin (GLY), potassium bromide (KBr), N,N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline (DMNA) and 4-nitroaniline (NA) were purchased from

Jingchun Industry Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). In this study, all of the above reagents were of analytical grade.

Guar bean gum (GG) and locust bean gum (LBG) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (USA) with the weight average molecular mass (Mw) of 2.25 x 10^6 g/mol and 8.65 x 10^5 g/mol, and polydispersity (PD) of 1.098 and 1.245, respectively. The monosaccharide composition of GG and LBG were D-mannose and D-galactose (M/G ratio of 1.20:1 and 3.63:1, respectively).

## 2.2. Computational methods Initial geometry optimizations of DESs and galactomannan model compounds were obtained using the B3LYP exchange-correlation function combined with the 6-311G (d, p) basis set (Pritchard, Altarawy, Didier, Gibson, & Windus, 2019; Stephens, Devlin, Chabalowski, & Frisch, 1994). To eliminate the dispersion effect, we added the key word of empirical dispersion = GD3BJ in the route section. Then, the initial structure of optimized DESs were performed at HF/6311G (d, p) level, and further reoptimized using the M06-2X exchange-correlation function in combination the 6-31++G (d, p) basis set based on the Gaussian 16 program package (Walker, Harvey, Sen, & Dessent, 2013). Given Gaussian results, the electrostatic surface potential (ESP) (Zhang & Lu, 2021), atom in molecules (AIM) (Bader, 1985), reduced density gradient (RDG) (Johnson et al., 2010) and frontline molecular orbitals (FMO) theory analyses were performed using the Multiwfn 3.8 programs (Lu & Chen, 2012). All the ESP, AIM and FMO maps were rendered by Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD) 1.9.4 program. The data of RDG was visualized by VMD 1.9.4 and Gnuplot 5.4.3 software.

All molecular dynamics (MD) details were performed in Gromacs 2022.3, and all studied molecules were parameterized using the charm 36 force field (AitRaise et al., 2023; Xu, Kong, Peng, Wang, & Li, 2021). The (4M-1G)-C1E4 system consisted of 186 ChCl molecules, 744 EG molecules and one 4M-1G models molecular chain. The C1E4 compo- nents were added to a 6 nm × 6 nm × 6 nm box in a certain amount and proportion. Periodic boundary condition (PBC) was applied to the three directions of the box to ensure that the number of particles in the box was constant. Under certain temperature and pressure conditions, the steepest descent method was used to simulate the system in 50000 steps to minimize the energy of the system. Then the systems were equili- brated for 100 ps under NVT ensemble with temperature at 300 K. Following was a 100 ps simulation under NPT ensemble to equilibrate the solvents. Finally, a long-term MD simulation with a step size of 250 million steps and a duration of 500 ns was carried out at constant temperature and constant pressure.

### 2.3. Preparation of DESs First, all relevant materials were dried before preparation. Then, mixing HBAs with corresponding HBDs according to the molar ratio provided in Table S3 to prepare type II DESs. The mixture in the sealed bottle was stirred with a magnetic stirrer and heated at 80 °C until clear homogeneous liquid was obtained (Ramezani, Ahmadi, & Yamini, 2022).

The preparation of *type III* DESs entailed weighing the corresponding components according to their composition and proportion, followed by stirring at 80 °C until a homogeneous and transparent liquid was formed.

2.4. Polarity determination of type II DESS Polarity scale (EN T), π* (dipolarity/polarizability), β (hydrogen bond basicity) and α (hydrogen bond acidity) values were calculated according to modified Kamlet-Taft empirical polarity scales (Ranjkesh, Parast, Strzeżysz, Zakerhamidi, & Yoon, 2018).

2.5. Measurement of viscosity The viscosity of the polysaccharide solution was measured using an Anton Paar Physica MCR 301 Rheometer (Anton Paar, GmbH, Austria) equipped with a cone-plate geometry (50 mm diameter). Samples were loaded onto a smooth Peltier plate which maintained constant experimental temperatures of 90 °C (±0.1 °C) for the studies presented herein. The plate spacing was 1 mm and temperature equilibration of the samples was achieved within 5 min prior to each measurement (Potier, Tea, Benyahia, Nicolai, & Renou, 2020). For each polysaccharide solution, steady shear and dynamic oscillatory shear experiments were carried out in the shear rate range of 0.1–1000 s⁻¹ and frequency range of 0.1–100 rad/s, respectively. All rheological data were analyzed with rheoplus software (Rheoplus/32 V3.40).

## 2.6. Solubility of galactomannans in different solvents The detailed measurement procedure for the solubility of galactomannans was based on the study by Cao et al. (Cao, Nian, Li, Wu, & Liu, 2019). Specifically, the dissolution process involved accurately weighing galactomannans (4 g ± 0.1 mg) into different solvents (60 mL ± 0.1 mL) and stirring the mixture magnetically at 80 °C for 5 h. The dissolved sample was centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 30 min, and the supernatant was collected. The supernatant was diluted 50 times with deionized water. Then, 1 mL of deionized water and 1 mL of 6% (w/v) phenol were added and mixed thoroughly. Next, 5 mL concentrated sulfuric acid was added to the mixture and fully mixed. After standing for 30 min, the absorption spectrum of the mixture at 490 nm was measured and calculated according to the following equation: $S = (A_{490nm}-b)/a \times 0.9 \times 10$ (1) Where $S$ represented the solubility of galactomannans (g/100 g), the absorbance of the mixture at 490 nm was expressed as $A_{490nm}$, the slope and intercept of the standard curve were expressed as $a$ and $b$. The standard curve was obtained by dissolving 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 g of glucose into 10 g of different DESs according to the above procedure. The determination process was performed in triplicate. The experimental data were analyzed using SPSS V.17.0 (p < 0.05).

## 2.7. Polarized light microscope 4 g GG and LBG were put into 60 mL different DESs, respectively, and stirred at 80 °C for 6–8 h. Dip a drop of GG solution onto a glass slide with a glass rod and observe it with a polarizing microscope (Axio scope A1, Carl Zeiss, Germany).

2.8. *Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy* The spectra were recorded at the wavenumber range of 4000–400 cm⁻¹ with FT-IR spectrophotometer (iS10, Thermo Nicolet, USA). The number of scans was 16 and referenced against air. The resolution of FT-IR was 4 cm⁻¹ (Beratto-Ramos, Agurto-Muñoz, Vargas-Montalba, & Castillo, 2020).

2.9. *NMR spectroscopy* ¹H and ¹H–¹H COSY NMR spectra were recorded at 25 °C by a Bruker Avance DPX-400 spectrometer (Bruker, Rheinstetten, Germany). Chemical shifts were reported in ppm using TMS as the internal reference. The NMR spectra of DESs and polysaccharides were determined in DMSO-d₆ and D₂O, respectively (Holding, King, & Kilpeläinen, 2018).
2.10. *Monosaccharide composition analysis* The sample (10 mg) was hydrolyzed with trifluoroacetic acid under

nitrogen protection at 120 °C for 8 h. The residual trifluoroacetic acid was removed by rotary evaporation. The hydrolysis product was added with ammonium hydrochloride (10 mg) and pyridine (1 mL) and reacted at 90 °C for 30 min. After cooling to room temperature, 1 mL of acetic anhydride was added and reacted at 90 °C for 30 min. The final product was extracted with 1 mL of chloroform and filtered through a 0.22 µm filter. The ensuing analysis was conducted by gas chromatograph (GC7900, Shanghai Tianmei Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd.).

## 2.11. Molecular mass analysis The molecular mass of the sample (1 mg/mL) was determined via size-exclusion chromatography combined with multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALLS). The sample was filtered through a 0.45 µm cellulose filter and eluted by an Ultrahydrogel™ column (7.8 × 300 mm, Waters, USA) with ultrapure water as mobile phase. The injection volume and flow rate were 50 µL and 0.5 mL/min, respectively. Zimm method was used to calculate the weight average molecular mass (M₇) and data analysis was performed using Astra software (Wyatt Tech. Corp., USA).
### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Dissolution of galactomannans in type II DESs
The effect of molecular weight and distribution pattern of Gal sub- stituents dissolution on DESs dissolution have attracted great attention.

The hydrogen bonding strength in galactomannans and traditional type II DESs was comparative studied by the atom in molecule (AIM) theory, thereby evaluating the potential solubility of GG and LBG (Fig. 1). The H-bonding strengths of traditional type II DESs and galactomannans were calculated at atomic level using 4M-2G and 4M-1G as sugar chain fragment models for GG and LBG. Typically, electron density (ρ) and its Laplacian (∇²ρ) could quantify the properties of hydrogen bonds which was shown in ranges from 0.02 to 0.15 au and 0.002 to 0.04 au for ∇²ρ and ρ, respectively (Lipkowski, Grabowski, Robinson, & Leszczynski, 2004). The ρ values of 4M-2G and 4M-1G models were 0.035 ~ 0.005 au and 0.037 ~ 0.004 au (Table S2), which were larger than those of ChCl-2EG (C1E2, 0.026 ~ 0.008 au) and ChCl-2Urea (C1U2, 0.023 ~ 0.017 au). Furthermore, the absolute values of hydrogen binding energy (|E_HB|) for 4M-2G and 4M-1G models, C1E2 and C1U2 were calculated (Fig. 1) and employed to reflect the types of hydrogen bond strength (Emamian, Lu, Kruse, & Emamian, 2019). According to the |E_HB|, it could be divided into strong (|E_HB| > 15.0 kcal/mol), medium (11 < |E_HB| < 15 kcal/mol), weak to medium (2.5 kcal/mol < |E_HB| < 14.0 kcal/mol) and weak (|E_HB| < 2.5 kcal/mol) H-bond. |E_HB| of C1E2 and C1U2 had weak to medium H-bonds, which were higher than 4M-2G and 4M-1G models. Based on the above results of AIM and |E_HB|, it was predicted that C1E2 and C1U2 could break the hydrogen bond network of LBG and GG, thus reflecting a certain solubility. These findings were consistent with the results of previous research. FT-IR spectroscopy and ¹H NMR were used to explore the H-bond interaction of DESs. All details were listed in Fig. S1. In type II DESs, C1E4 was taken as an example to analyze the specific characterization results. It could be clearly observed from the FT-IR spectra that the hydroxyl groups on ChCl and EG had blue-shifted from 3255 and 3357–3374 cm⁻¹, respectively, indicating that the interaction between ChCl and EG had resulted in an increase in the vibration frequency of the chemical bond and the formation of new hydrogen bonds. Similar phenomena had been reported in research conducted by Feng et al. (Feng et al., 2022) and Zhu et al. (Zhu et al., 2016), where hydrogen bond interactions between HBD and HBA in DESs could lead to blue shifts in FT-IR spectra. This further confirmed the universality and significance of this phenomenon within DES systems. In addition, as shown ¹H NMR spectra, compared with ChCl, the hydrogen atom of H-1 shifted from 5.74 to 5.46 ppm. Meanwhile, the H-5 located on EG was found to be low field shifted from 4.52 to 4.56 ppm. These results illustrated the H-bond interaction between ChCl and EG.

Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters were utilized as quantitative tool to measure the polarity of DESs (Fig. 2c and Fig. S3). These parameters effectively assessed the hydrogen-bond donating ability (acidity, α), hydrogen-bond accepting ability (basicity, β), and polarity/polarizability (π*) of C1E4. The comparison of C1E2 and ChCl–4EG (C1E4) showed that the α values of C1E4 was improved to 0.917, such high values indicated that it was easy to release H⁺. The π* values

exhibited a decrease to 1.077 suggesting that the solubility of C1E4 was higher compared to C1E2. Similar findings had also been reported by Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2023). Their results showed that lignin sol-ubility had a closed positive correlation with the subtraction value of α and β of DESs. Among all the investigated DESs, L-alanine/formic acid (1:3) with the strong hydrogen-bond donating ability, weak hydrogen-bond accepting ability and small steric-hindrance effect showed the best lignin dissolving ability. Therefore, the H-bond accepting and dissolving capacity of the solvent increased after improving proportion of EG.

It was apparent that the solubilities of LBG and GG were greatly higher in type II DESs than in conventional solvent, the maximum sol-ubility of GG was 0.28 g/100 mL and the minimum was 0.02 g/100 mL in type II DESs for instance. Surprisingly, the solubility of LBG was approximately 28 times higher compared to GG (Fig. 2a). Meanwhile, the viscosity followed the order: GG solutions > LBG solutions > type II DESs at the same temperature (Fig. 2c and Fig. S2). These results proved that galactomannans had different solubilization consequences in the same DESs, which was dependent on the molecular weight and degree of branching. Upon examination under a polarizing microscope (Fig. 2b), the solutions of LBG and GG in DESs exhibited complete dark field, signifying that LBG and GG were fully dissolved in the DESs, resulting in an optically transparent solution. In addition, the solution showed a uniform appearance with no visible particles or precipitates, further confirming the effective dissolution of LBG and GG in C1E2 and C1E4. Investigation of H-bonding interactions of DES by DFT calculation TheThe different qualities of H-bonds in DESs lead to the difficulties associated with the quantification of H-bonding interactions. Here, DFT calculation was employed to gain an insight into the H-bonding interactions of DESs at an atomic level. The optimized structures of ChCl, EG and C1E4 were shown in Fig. 3a. The choline cation (Ch⁺) might be considered as a tetrahedron formed by the methyl/methylene groups of a quaternary ammonium head and a CH₂OH chain extending from one of the vertices and partially blocking the corresponding face. Additionally, two hydroxyl groups in the EG endowed the C1E4 with numerous H-bond interacting capabilities. Thus, the main types of H-bonding in C1E4 identified as: cationic H-bond (Ch⁺ and EG), anionic H-bond (Cl⁻ and EG), doubly ionic H-bond (ChCl ion pairs), and neutral H-bond (EG - EG).

AIM theory could quantify the H-bond interactions at bond critical points (BCPs) in accordance with ρ and ∇²ρ. The topological diagram of C1E4 exhibited by AIM investigation (Fig. 3a), and summarized the

Design of type III DESs to promote galactomannans dissolution To further enhance the dissolution of galactomannans, AlCl3·6H2O as an anion donor and active acidic site holder was introduced in C1E2 to predict the solubility of type III DESs (Fig. 9a). AIM theory showed that ρ values of 4M-2G and 4M-1G models were 0.035 ~ 0.005 au and 0.037 ~ 0.004 au (Table S3), which were smaller than those of C1E2-AlCl3·6H2O (0.038 ~ 0.005 au). Moreover, |EHB| of C1E2- AlCl3·6H2O had a large number of weak to medium H-bonds, which were higher than 4M-2G and 4M-1G models. Hence, C1E2- AlCl3·6H2O broke the H-bonds network of LBG and GG, and reflecting a certain solubility.

## 4. Conclusion In this work, to elucidate how DES components affect the dissolution of polysaccharides with variable molecular weight and Gal substituent distribution, a systematic investigation was conducted using DFT calculation prediction, MD, and characterization of type II/III DESs and recovered galactomannans. Among the examined DESs, C1E4 with a high proportion of HBDs exhibited remarkable solubility by providing more H-bond sites. This result explained by the fact that C1E4 with a large number of anionic and neutral H-bonds broke the original galactomannan H-bond networks and rebuilt new hydrogen bonds. The solubility of galactomannans was related to its molecular weight and distribution pattern of Gal substituents, which could be explained that the repulsive interactions hindered H-bonds breaking due to the high molecular weight and rich Gal side-chains ("hairy" regions) for GG, resulting low solubility (0.16 g/100 mL). Additionally, it was indicated that immense number of active acid sites in type III DESs not only effectively broke and rebuilt the galactomannans H-bond networks, but also cleaved the glycosidic bond to obtain recovered polysaccharides with target molecular weight. Taken together, this work provided a promising strategy for development of task specific DESs and their widespread polysaccharide resources application in the future.

The cover features various scientific illustrations including a chain-like structure, spherical clusters, complex molecular structures, and microscopic images of materials : figure::> <::logo: Check for updates A square button with a gray background and a red bookmark icon inside a blue and yellow circle::> The dissolution of galactomannans in _type II/III_ deep eutectic solvents: Effect of polysaccharide structure and interaction mechanism Duoduo Guoⁿ, Jinfeng Hanⁿ, Hui Tangⁿ, Yaxu Sunⁿ, Li Liⁿ,⁻, Weibao Kongⁿ,⁽,ⁿ, Junyu Liangⁿ,⁽,ⁿ, Ji Zhangⁿ,⁽,ⁿ, Junlong Wangⁿ,⁽,ⁿ,* a _College of Life Science, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou, 730070, China_ b _Gansu Provincial Hospital, Lanzhou, 730000, China_ c _Functional Food Technology Innovation Center of Gansu Province, Lanzhou, 730070, China_ d _Institute of New Rural Development, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou, 730070, China_ ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Galactomannans Deep eutectic solvents Dissolution mechanism Computational quantum chemistry # ABSTRACT Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have garnered increasing attention as sustainable solvents for natural polysaccharides. Galactomannans (especially guar and locust bean gums) are abundant natural compounds used in food, medicine, agriculture and daily chemical products, whereas their high molecular weight and randomly distributed non-linear structures remain a huge challenge in solubilization and high value-added utilization. In this study, the dissolution of galactomannans in type II/III DESs was comprehensively investigated using density functional theory (DFT) calculation, experimental results, and molecular dynamics simulation (MD). The results indicated that immense anionic and neutral H-bonds supported by type II DESs (consisting of a quaternary ammonium salt and a metal chloride hydrate) could break and rebuild galactomannan H-bond networks, thereby exhibiting remarkable physical solubilization. A large number of active acid sites in type III DESs (consisting of a quaternary ammonium salt and a hydrogen bond donor) greatly improved solubility and cleaved the glycosidic bond, enabling the recovery of polysaccharides with a target molecular weight. Furthermore, significant correlations between solubility and the structure of galactomannans had been established, which meant that high molecular weight and rich galactose side-chains produced repulsive interactions with DESs, directly hindering dissolution. Overall, this work not only offered a framework for enhancing the dissolution of polysaccharides, but also proposed a promising strategy for development of task specific DESs promoting green chemistry and the use of sustainable bioresources. ## 1. Introduction The application of natural polysaccharides in food, medicine, ma-terials and fuels have become an attractive option over the past few decades to mitigate increasing demands for resources in modern society and the promotion of environmental protection (Schlemmer, Selinger, Hobisch, & Spirk, 2021). Due to their biocompatible and biodegradable properties, polysaccharides have been utilized as building blocks to yield polysaccharide-based hydrogels through physical and/or chemical crosslinking of polysaccharides via a variety of monomers or ions. These polysaccharide-derived hydrogels exhibit peculiar physicochemical properties and excellent mechanical properties due to their unique structures and abundant functional groups. (Manzoor et al., 2022). Additionally, cellulose, starch and gel polysaccharides (e.g. galactomannans) as structural polysaccharides, are commonly used in biomedical fields including bone tissue engineering, cosmetic, food, antibacterial agents etc (Gopinath et al., 2022; Prajapati et al., 2013). Attentions have been paid by galactomannans which exhibit bio- activities such as reducing calorie intakes, controlling blood glucose, and reducing the risks of heart diseases and colon cancer (Li & Nie, 2016; Singh et al., 2021). Galactomannans possess a linear \u03b2-1,4-linked D-mannose backbone to which D-galactose residues are linked by \u03b1-1,6 glycosidic linkages (Moreira & Filho, 2008). In galactomannan family, the chemical structure for each member varies depending on the ratio of mannose to galactose (M/G). For example, the M/G ratio is approxi- mately 4:1 for locust bean gum (LBG, from Ceratonia siliqua) and 2:1 for guar gum (GG, from Cyamopsis tetragonolobus) (Liu et al., 2020; Niknam, Mousavi, & Kiani, 2022). Food Hydrocolloids 158 (2025) 110552 fine structure of galactomannans is composed of "smooth" zones (lowly substituted) and "hairy" zones (highly substituted), which leads to a dense intra/inter hydrogen bonds networks (Grisel, Aguni, Renou, & Malhiac, 2015). As a result, it is difficult to dissolve in H2O (highly swollen) and traditional organic solvents (dimethyl sulfoxide, form- amide, etc.) that suffers from volatility and flammability, which makes the task specific functionalization very difficult (Depoorter et al., 2019). Thus, a novel, efficient and green solvent system for the functional proliferation of galactomannan is in urgent demand. Nowadays, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) with low volatility, high designability and low toxicity are considered to have striking applica- tion potential in the processing of natural polysaccharides (Zdanowicz, Wilpiszewska, & Spychaj, 2018). A large number of studies have shown that DESs can achieve efficient solubilization of polysaccharides compared with traditional solvents due to their green characteristics and adjustable physical and chemical properties (Liu et al., 2023). The application of DESs in polysaccharide extraction has great advantages which increases the extraction rate of polysaccharides compared with traditional solvents (Table S1), as reported in extraction of Lycium bar- barum (1.74-fold higher) and Schisandra chinensis polysaccharides (1.39-fold higher) (Gu, Lin, & Zhao, 2023; Yan et al., 2023). This can be explained by the fact that DESs featured by multiple hydrogen bond sites, which provide the abilities to occur hydrogen bonding interaction between DESs and polysaccharides, thereby achieving the purpose of efficient polysaccharides extraction (Pan et al., 2022; Zheng, Hu, Tu, & Wu, 2023). In addition, the task specific functionalization of natural polysaccharides by DESs is an important way to further its high-value utilization. Recent studies have shown that different types of surface chemical functionalization on the cellulose nanofibrils are obtained by using DESs to swell cellulose fibers and weaken of hydrogen bonding network, which confer to the final material distinct properties (Almeida, Maloney, & Gamelas, 2023). Meantime, our previous studies have also confirmed DES/DMSO binary mixed solvents boosting Se-functionalization by enhanced solubilization of hetero- polysaccharide, which is attributed to the disruption of original hydrogen bond networks of polysaccharide, allowing the DESs within the system to interact more easily with polysaccharides (Sun et al., 2022). As is well-known, polysaccharides possess very high structural specificity, including molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, conformation, etc. However, it is important to note that most studies focus primarily on the application of DESs in the field of polysaccharide processing, with limited research conducted on the correlation of DES components with the structure of polysaccharides and the potential dissolution differences (Guo et al., 2021; Prasad & Sharma, 2019). In addition, some researchers have shown that acidic DESs can cause the degradation of polysaccharides, namely, the breaking of glycosidic bonds and the decrease of molecular weight (Yang et al., 2022). One such example is a study by Tian et al. (Tian et al., 2020), who used ChCl-oxalic acid (ChCl-OA) to treat cellulose. As a result, the acidity in ChCl-OA can provide H protons, thus breaking the glycosidic bond and finally obtaining several oligosaccharides linked by β-1,4-glucosidase bonds. The primary issue, therefore, is the relative lack of research on the structure of recovered polysaccharide after DESs treatment. Increased attention on the importance of this topic should attract a research model that systematically compares the dissolution relation- ship between DESs and recovered polysaccharide structure, to prove the physical or chemical dissolution of polysaccharides by DESs. As discussed above, DESs have the advantage of designability. Based on this feature, an approach of expanding DESs function is the intro- duction of Lewis acid into the conventional _type II_ DESs to prepare _type_ _III_ DESs, which is considered to have great application potential in the field of biomass processing. Using ChCl/glycerol (1:2) as an example, Xia and co-workers show that this system is unable to cleave ether bond linkages in lignin-carbohydrate complexes due to the absence of active protons and acidic sites. Accordingly, based on an acidic multisite co- ordination theory, the _type III_ DESs are designed. The competition of anionic H-bonds and unidentate aluminum ligands is synchronized to form supramolecular complexes, allowing the multisite bridging ligands to cleave both the H-bonds and ether bonds in lignin-carbohydrate complexes, and the purity of extracted lignin is as high as 94 % (Xia et al., 2018). Additionally, high viscosity is one of the main obstacles to the further application of DESs. The addition of aprotic solvent as the third component to type II DESs can effectively reduce the viscosity of conventional DESs for the further processing and utilization of polysaccharides. For example, the addition of DMSO as a cosolvent to traditional type II DESs can reduce the viscosity and increase the reactivity, which greatly improves the effective conversion of sugar bagasse into platform chemicals (Amesho et al., 2022). Almost simultaneously, it is reported that the conversion rate of hexose in corn stover was significantly increased from 10.95% to 41.40% by using DMSO to reduce the viscosity of ChCl:oxalic acid (Lu et al., 2022). However, given the immense number of HBAs and HBDs, finding "optimal" eutectic mixtures for a given application will currently exhaustive trial-and-error through millions of possible binary combinations (Hansen et al., 2020). This is one of the reasons why the current type III DESs are mostly limited to the treatment of cellulose, and the application of other polysaccharides is less. Moreover, on the one hand, the type III DESs by introducing Lewis acid will form strong anions (OH…Cl) and neutral hydrogen bonds (OH…O), which will break the glycosidic bond of polysaccharides (Ji, Yu, Wu, et al., 2021; Zhou, Fakayode, Yagoub, Ji, & Zhou, 2022); on the other hand, it responds to the molecular weight, branching degree and crystallinity of complex polysaccharides, resulting in different dissolution results. While type III DESs have demonstrated excellent properties in extracting cellulose from biomass, research on type III DESs is still in its early stages (Bai, Zhang, Wang, Zheng, & Yao, 2022; Zhang, Wu, Wang, Li, & Fang, 2024). Particularly, reports on the potential solubilization ability of type III DES in polysaccharides treatment, are rare. Moreover, the influence of type III DESs composition and proportion on the structure of the recovered polysaccharide are not well elucidated, which hinder the development of DESs and their utilization in polysaccharides dissolution and functionalization. As such, a primary objective of current research is to comparatively evaluate the dissolution relationship between polysaccharide structures and DES components, and to adapt DESs for specific applications. In this work, two typical galactomannans (LBG and GG), with same linear ẞ-1,4-linked D-mannose backbone but different M/G and molecular weight, were employed to study the effect of molecular weight and distribution pattern of Gal substituents on DESs dissolution. First, density functional theory (DFT) calculation was performed to predict the dissolution effects of GG and LBG fragment models in several traditional type II DESs. After preparing and characterizing a series of type II DESs, the optimal type II DES was screened from viscosity, polarity and solubility to LBG and GG. Subsequently, the dissolution mechanism of type II DESs on galactomannans was elucidated by DFT, molecular dynamics simulation (MD) and structural characterization of recovered polysaccharides. Taking advantage of DESs designability, type III DESs with AlCl3-6H2O as the third component were employed to achieve efficient dissolution of galactomannans. The effect of type III DESs with Lewis acid on the structure of the galactomannans during the solubilization was further evaluated by structural characterization of recovered galactomannans. This study aimed to explore the dissolution relationship between polysaccharides structure and DES components, to provide reference for the realization of DESs task specific functionalization and to fully utilize polysaccharide resources. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Choline chloride (ChCl), ethylene glycol (EG), urea, 1,4-butanediol (BDO), glycerin (GLY), potassium bromide (KBr), N,N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline (DMNA) and 4-nitroaniline (NA) were purchased from 2 D. Guo et al. Food Hydrocolloids 158 (2025) 110552 Jingchun Industry Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). In this study, all of the above reagents were of analytical grade. Guar bean gum (GG) and locust bean gum (LBG) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (USA) with the weight average molecular mass (Mw) of 2.25 x 10^6 g/mol and 8.65 x 10^5 g/mol, and polydispersity (PD) of 1.098 and 1.245, respectively. The monosaccharide composition of GG and LBG were D-mannose and D-galactose (M/G ratio of 1.20:1 and 3.63:1, respectively). ## 2.2. Computational methods Initial geometry optimizations of DESs and galactomannan model compounds were obtained using the B3LYP exchange-correlation function combined with the 6-311G (d, p) basis set (Pritchard, Altarawy, Didier, Gibson, & Windus, 2019; Stephens, Devlin, Chabalowski, & Frisch, 1994). To eliminate the dispersion effect, we added the key word of empirical dispersion = GD3BJ in the route section. Then, the initial structure of optimized DESs were performed at HF/6311G (d, p) level, and further reoptimized using the M06-2X exchange-correlation function in combination the 6-31++G (d, p) basis set based on the Gaussian 16 program package (Walker, Harvey, Sen, & Dessent, 2013). Given Gaussian results, the electrostatic surface potential (ESP) (Zhang & Lu, 2021), atom in molecules (AIM) (Bader, 1985), reduced density gradient (RDG) (Johnson et al., 2010) and frontline molecular orbitals (FMO) theory analyses were performed using the Multiwfn 3.8 programs (Lu & Chen, 2012). All the ESP, AIM and FMO maps were rendered by Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD) 1.9.4 program. The data of RDG was visualized by VMD 1.9.4 and Gnuplot 5.4.3 software. All molecular dynamics (MD) details were performed in Gromacs 2022.3, and all studied molecules were parameterized using the charm 36 force field (AitRaise et al., 2023; Xu, Kong, Peng, Wang, & Li, 2021). The (4M-1G)-C1E4 system consisted of 186 ChCl molecules, 744 EG molecules and one 4M-1G models molecular chain. The C1E4 compo- nents were added to a 6 nm × 6 nm × 6 nm box in a certain amount and proportion. Periodic boundary condition (PBC) was applied to the three directions of the box to ensure that the number of particles in the box was constant. Under certain temperature and pressure conditions, the steepest descent method was used to simulate the system in 50000 steps to minimize the energy of the system. Then the systems were equili- brated for 100 ps under NVT ensemble with temperature at 300 K. Following was a 100 ps simulation under NPT ensemble to equilibrate the solvents. Finally, a long-term MD simulation with a step size of 250 million steps and a duration of 500 ns was carried out at constant temperature and constant pressure. ### 2.3. Preparation of DESs First, all relevant materials were dried before preparation. Then, mixing HBAs with corresponding HBDs according to the molar ratio provided in Table S3 to prepare type II DESs. The mixture in the sealed bottle was stirred with a magnetic stirrer and heated at 80 °C until clear homogeneous liquid was obtained (Ramezani, Ahmadi, & Yamini, 2022). The preparation of *type III* DESs entailed weighing the corresponding components according to their composition and proportion, followed by stirring at 80 °C until a homogeneous and transparent liquid was formed. 2.4. Polarity determination of type II DESS Polarity scale (EN T), π* (dipolarity/polarizability), β (hydrogen bond basicity) and α (hydrogen bond acidity) values were calculated according to modified Kamlet-Taft empirical polarity scales (Ranjkesh, Parast, Strzeżysz, Zakerhamidi, & Yoon, 2018). 2.5. Measurement of viscosity The viscosity of the polysaccharide solution was measured using an Anton Paar Physica MCR 301 Rheometer (Anton Paar, GmbH, Austria) equipped with a cone-plate geometry (50 mm diameter). Samples were loaded onto a smooth Peltier plate which maintained constant experimental temperatures of 90 °C (±0.1 °C) for the studies presented herein. The plate spacing was 1 mm and temperature equilibration of the samples was achieved within 5 min prior to each measurement (Potier, Tea, Benyahia, Nicolai, & Renou, 2020). For each polysaccharide solution, steady shear and dynamic oscillatory shear experiments were carried out in the shear rate range of 0.1–1000 s⁻¹ and frequency range of 0.1–100 rad/s, respectively. All rheological data were analyzed with rheoplus software (Rheoplus/32 V3.40). ## 2.6. Solubility of galactomannans in different solvents The detailed measurement procedure for the solubility of galactomannans was based on the study by Cao et al. (Cao, Nian, Li, Wu, & Liu, 2019). Specifically, the dissolution process involved accurately weighing galactomannans (4 g ± 0.1 mg) into different solvents (60 mL ± 0.1 mL) and stirring the mixture magnetically at 80 °C for 5 h. The dissolved sample was centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 30 min, and the supernatant was collected. The supernatant was diluted 50 times with deionized water. Then, 1 mL of deionized water and 1 mL of 6% (w/v) phenol were added and mixed thoroughly. Next, 5 mL concentrated sulfuric acid was added to the mixture and fully mixed. After standing for 30 min, the absorption spectrum of the mixture at 490 nm was measured and calculated according to the following equation: $S = (A_{490nm}-b)/a \times 0.9 \times 10$ (1) Where $S$ represented the solubility of galactomannans (g/100 g), the absorbance of the mixture at 490 nm was expressed as $A_{490nm}$, the slope and intercept of the standard curve were expressed as $a$ and $b$. The standard curve was obtained by dissolving 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 g of glucose into 10 g of different DESs according to the above procedure. The determination process was performed in triplicate. The experimental data were analyzed using SPSS V.17.0 (p < 0.05). ## 2.7. Polarized light microscope 4 g GG and LBG were put into 60 mL different DESs, respectively, and stirred at 80 °C for 6–8 h. Dip a drop of GG solution onto a glass slide with a glass rod and observe it with a polarizing microscope (Axio scope A1, Carl Zeiss, Germany). 2.8. *Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy* The spectra were recorded at the wavenumber range of 4000–400 cm⁻¹ with FT-IR spectrophotometer (iS10, Thermo Nicolet, USA). The number of scans was 16 and referenced against air. The resolution of FT-IR was 4 cm⁻¹ (Beratto-Ramos, Agurto-Muñoz, Vargas-Montalba, & Castillo, 2020). 2.9. *NMR spectroscopy* ¹H and ¹H–¹H COSY NMR spectra were recorded at 25 °C by a Bruker Avance DPX-400 spectrometer (Bruker, Rheinstetten, Germany). Chemical shifts were reported in ppm using TMS as the internal reference. The NMR spectra of DESs and polysaccharides were determined in DMSO-d₆ and D₂O, respectively (Holding, King, & Kilpeläinen, 2018). 2.10. *Monosaccharide composition analysis* The sample (10 mg) was hydrolyzed with trifluoroacetic acid under 3 D. Guo et al. Food Hydrocolloids 158 (2025) 110552 nitrogen protection at 120 °C for 8 h. The residual trifluoroacetic acid was removed by rotary evaporation. The hydrolysis product was added with ammonium hydrochloride (10 mg) and pyridine (1 mL) and reacted at 90 °C for 30 min. After cooling to room temperature, 1 mL of acetic anhydride was added and reacted at 90 °C for 30 min. The final product was extracted with 1 mL of chloroform and filtered through a 0.22 µm filter. The ensuing analysis was conducted by gas chromatograph (GC7900, Shanghai Tianmei Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd.). ## 2.11. Molecular mass analysis The molecular mass of the sample (1 mg/mL) was determined via size-exclusion chromatography combined with multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALLS). The sample was filtered through a 0.45 µm cellulose filter and eluted by an Ultrahydrogel™ column (7.8 × 300 mm, Waters, USA) with ultrapure water as mobile phase. The injection volume and flow rate were 50 µL and 0.5 mL/min, respectively. Zimm method was used to calculate the weight average molecular mass (M₇) and data analysis was performed using Astra software (Wyatt Tech. Corp., USA). ### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Dissolution of galactomannans in type II DESs The effect of molecular weight and distribution pattern of Gal sub- stituents dissolution on DESs dissolution have attracted great attention. The hydrogen bonding strength in galactomannans and traditional type II DESs was comparative studied by the atom in molecule (AIM) theory, thereby evaluating the potential solubility of GG and LBG (Fig. 1). The H-bonding strengths of traditional type II DESs and galactomannans were calculated at atomic level using 4M-2G and 4M-1G as sugar chain fragment models for GG and LBG. Typically, electron density (ρ) and its Laplacian (∇²ρ) could quantify the properties of hydrogen bonds which was shown in ranges from 0.02 to 0.15 au and 0.002 to 0.04 au for ∇²ρ and ρ, respectively (Lipkowski, Grabowski, Robinson, & Leszczynski, 2004). The ρ values of 4M-2G and 4M-1G models were 0.035 ~ 0.005 au and 0.037 ~ 0.004 au (Table S2), which were larger than those of ChCl-2EG (C1E2, 0.026 ~ 0.008 au) and ChCl-2Urea (C1U2, 0.023 ~ 0.017 au). Furthermore, the absolute values of hydrogen binding energy (|E_HB|) for 4M-2G and 4M-1G models, C1E2 and C1U2 were calculated (Fig. 1) and employed to reflect the types of hydrogen bond strength (Emamian, Lu, Kruse, & Emamian, 2019). Conclusion In this work, to elucidate how DES components affect the dissolution of polysaccharides with variable molecular weight and Gal substituent distribution, a systematic investigation was conducted using DFT calculation prediction, MD, and characterization of type II/III DESs and recovered galactomannans. Among the examined DESs, C1E4 with a high proportion of HBDs exhibited remarkable solubility by providing more H-bond sites. This result explained by the fact that C1E4 with a large number of anionic and neutral H-bonds broke the original galactomannan H-bond networks and rebuilt new hydrogen bonds. The solubility of galactomannans was related to its molecular weight and distribution pattern of Gal substituents, which could be explained that the repulsive interactions hindered H-bonds breaking due to the high molecular weight and rich Gal side-chains ("hairy" regions) for GG, resulting low solubility (0.16 g/100 mL). Additionally, it was indicated that immense number of active acid sites in type III DESs not only effectively broke and rebuilt the galactomannans H-bond networks, but also cleaved the glycosidic bond to obtain recovered polysaccharides with target molecular weight. Taken together, this work provided a promising strategy for development of task specific DESs and their widespread polysaccharide resources application in the future. The cover features various scientific illustrations including a chain-like structure, spherical clusters, complex molecular structures, and microscopic images of materials : figure::> <::logo: Check for updates A square button with a gray background and a red bookmark icon inside a blue and yellow circle::> The dissolution of galactomannans in _type II/III_ deep eutectic solvents: Effect of polysaccharide structure and interaction mechanism Duoduo Guoⁿ, Jinfeng Hanⁿ, Hui Tangⁿ, Yaxu Sunⁿ, Li Liⁿ,⁻, Weibao Kongⁿ,⁽,ⁿ, Junyu Liangⁿ,⁽,ⁿ, Ji Zhangⁿ,⁽,ⁿ, Junlong Wangⁿ,⁽,ⁿ,* a _College of Life Science, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou, 730070, China_ b _Gansu Provincial Hospital, Lanzhou, 730000, China_ c _Functional Food Technology Innovation Center of Gansu Province, Lanzhou, 730070, China_ d _Institute of New Rural Development, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou, 730070, China_ ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Galactomannans Deep eutectic solvents Dissolution mechanism Computational quantum chemistry # ABSTRACT Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have garnered increasing attention as sustainable solvents for natural polysaccharides. Galactomannans (especially guar and locust bean gums) are abundant natural compounds used in food, medicine, agriculture and daily chemical products, whereas their high molecular weight and randomly distributed non-linear structures remain a huge challenge in solubilization and high value-added utilization. In this study, the dissolution of galactomannans in type II/III DESs was comprehensively investigated using density functional theory (DFT) calculation, experimental results, and molecular dynamics simulation (MD). The results indicated that immense anionic and neutral H-bonds supported by type II DESs (consisting of a quaternary ammonium salt and a metal chloride hydrate) could break and rebuild galactomannan H-bond networks, thereby exhibiting remarkable physical solubilization. A large number of active acid sites in type III DESs (consisting of a quaternary ammonium salt and a hydrogen bond donor) greatly improved solubility and cleaved the glycosidic bond, enabling the recovery of polysaccharides with a target molecular weight. Furthermore, significant correlations between solubility and the structure of galactomannans had been established, which meant that high molecular weight and rich galactose side-chains produced repulsive interactions with DESs, directly hindering dissolution. Overall, this work not only offered a framework for enhancing the dissolution of polysaccharides, but also proposed a promising strategy for development of task specific DESs promoting green chemistry and the use of sustainable bioresources. ## 1. Introduction The application of natural polysaccharides in food, medicine, ma-terials and fuels have become an attractive option over the past few decades to mitigate increasing demands for resources in modern society and the promotion of environmental protection (Schlemmer, Selinger, Hobisch, & Spirk, 2021). Due to their biocompatible and biodegradable properties, polysaccharides have been utilized as building blocks to yield polysaccharide-based hydrogels through physical and/or chemical crosslinking of polysaccharides via a variety of monomers or ions. These polysaccharide-derived hydrogels exhibit peculiar physicochemical properties and excellent mechanical properties due to their unique structures and abundant functional groups. (Manzoor et al., 2022). Additionally, cellulose, starch and gel polysaccharides (e.g. galactomannans) as structural polysaccharides, are commonly used in biomedical fields including bone tissue engineering, cosmetic, food, antibacterial agents etc (Gopinath et al., 2022; Prajapati et al., 2013). Attentions have been paid by galactomannans which exhibit bio- activities such as reducing calorie intakes, controlling blood glucose, and reducing the risks of heart diseases and colon cancer (Li & Nie, 2016; Singh et al., 2021). Galactomannans possess a linear \u03b2-1,4-linked D-mannose backbone to which D-galactose residues are linked by \u03b1-1,6 glycosidic linkages (Moreira & Filho, 2008). In galactomannan family, the chemical structure for each member varies depending on the ratio of mannose to galactose (M/G). For example, the M/G ratio is approxi- mately 4:1 for locust bean gum (LBG, from Ceratonia siliqua) and 2:1 for guar gum (GG, from Cyamopsis tetragonolobus) (Liu et al., 2020; Niknam, Mousavi, & Kiani, 2022). Food Hydrocolloids 158 (2025) 110552 fine structure of galactomannans is composed of "smooth" zones (lowly substituted) and "hairy" zones (highly substituted), which leads to a dense intra/inter hydrogen bonds networks (Grisel, Aguni, Renou, & Malhiac, 2015). As a result, it is difficult to dissolve in H2O (highly swollen) and traditional organic solvents (dimethyl sulfoxide, form- amide, etc.) that suffers from volatility and flammability, which makes the task specific functionalization very difficult (Depoorter et al., 2019). Thus, a novel, efficient and green solvent system for the functional proliferation of galactomannan is in urgent demand. Nowadays, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) with low volatility, high designability and low toxicity are considered to have striking applica- tion potential in the processing of natural polysaccharides (Zdanowicz, Wilpiszewska, & Spychaj, 2018). A large number of studies have shown that DESs can achieve efficient solubilization of polysaccharides compared with traditional solvents due to their green characteristics and adjustable physical and chemical properties (Liu et al., 2023). The application of DESs in polysaccharide extraction has great advantages which increases the extraction rate of polysaccharides compared with traditional solvents (Table S1), as reported in extraction of Lycium bar- barum (1.74-fold higher) and Schisandra chinensis polysaccharides (1.39-fold higher) (Gu, Lin, & Zhao, 2023; Yan et al., 2023). This can be explained by the fact that DESs featured by multiple hydrogen bond sites, which provide the abilities to occur hydrogen bonding interaction between DESs and polysaccharides, thereby achieving the purpose of efficient polysaccharides extraction (Pan et al., 2022; Zheng, Hu, Tu, & Wu, 2023). In addition, the task specific functionalization of natural polysaccharides by DESs is an important way to further its high-value utilization. Recent studies have shown that different types of surface chemical functionalization on the cellulose nanofibrils are obtained by using DESs to swell cellulose fibers and weaken of hydrogen bonding network, which confer to the final material distinct properties (Almeida, Maloney, & Gamelas, 2023). Meantime, our previous studies have also confirmed DES/DMSO binary mixed solvents boosting Se-functionalization by enhanced solubilization of hetero- polysaccharide, which is attributed to the disruption of original hydrogen bond networks of polysaccharide, allowing the DESs within the system to interact more easily with polysaccharides (Sun et al., 2022). As is well-known, polysaccharides possess very high structural specificity, including molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, conformation, etc. However, it is important to note that most studies focus primarily on the application of DESs in the field of polysaccharide processing, with limited research conducted on the correlation of DES components with the structure of polysaccharides and the potential dissolution differences (Guo et al., 2021; Prasad & Sharma, 2019). In addition, some researchers have shown that acidic DESs can cause the degradation of polysaccharides, namely, the breaking of glycosidic bonds and the decrease of molecular weight (Yang et al., 2022). One such example is a study by Tian et al. (Tian et al., 2020), who used ChCl-oxalic acid (ChCl-OA) to treat cellulose. As a result, the acidity in ChCl-OA can provide H protons, thus breaking the glycosidic bond and finally obtaining several oligosaccharides linked by β-1,4-glucosidase bonds. The primary issue, therefore, is the relative lack of research on the structure of recovered polysaccharide after DESs treatment. Increased attention on the importance of this topic should attract a research model that systematically compares the dissolution relation- ship between DESs and recovered polysaccharide structure, to prove the physical or chemical dissolution of polysaccharides by DESs. As discussed above, DESs have the advantage of designability. Based on this feature, an approach of expanding DESs function is the intro- duction of Lewis acid into the conventional _type II_ DESs to prepare _type_ _III_ DESs, which is considered to have great application potential in the field of biomass processing. Using ChCl/glycerol (1:2) as an example, Xia and co-workers show that this system is unable to cleave ether bond linkages in lignin-carbohydrate complexes due to the absence of active protons and acidic sites. Accordingly, based on an acidic multisite co- ordination theory, the _type III_ DESs are designed. The competition of anionic H-bonds and unidentate aluminum ligands is synchronized to form supramolecular complexes, allowing the multisite bridging ligands to cleave both the H-bonds and ether bonds in lignin-carbohydrate complexes, and the purity of extracted lignin is as high as 94 % (Xia et al., 2018). Additionally, high viscosity is one of the main obstacles to the further application of DESs. The addition of aprotic solvent as the third component to type II DESs can effectively reduce the viscosity of conventional DESs for the further processing and utilization of polysaccharides. For example, the addition of DMSO as a cosolvent to traditional type II DESs can reduce the viscosity and increase the reactivity, which greatly improves the effective conversion of sugar bagasse into platform chemicals (Amesho et al., 2022). Almost simultaneously, it is reported that the conversion rate of hexose in corn stover was significantly increased from 10.95% to 41.40% by using DMSO to reduce the viscosity of ChCl:oxalic acid (Lu et al., 2022). However, given the immense number of HBAs and HBDs, finding "optimal" eutectic mixtures for a given application will currently exhaustive trial-and-error through millions of possible binary combinations (Hansen et al., 2020). This is one of the reasons why the current type III DESs are mostly limited to the treatment of cellulose, and the application of other polysaccharides is less. Moreover, on the one hand, the type III DESs by introducing Lewis acid will form strong anions (OH…Cl) and neutral hydrogen bonds (OH…O), which will break the glycosidic bond of polysaccharides (Ji, Yu, Wu, et al., 2021; Zhou, Fakayode, Yagoub, Ji, & Zhou, 2022); on the other hand, it responds to the molecular weight, branching degree and crystallinity of complex polysaccharides, resulting in different dissolution results. While type III DESs have demonstrated excellent properties in extracting cellulose from biomass, research on type III DESs is still in its early stages (Bai, Zhang, Wang, Zheng, & Yao, 2022; Zhang, Wu, Wang, Li, & Fang, 2024). Particularly, reports on the potential solubilization ability of type III DES in polysaccharides treatment, are rare. Moreover, the influence of type III DESs composition and proportion on the structure of the recovered polysaccharide are not well elucidated, which hinder the development of DESs and their utilization in polysaccharides dissolution and functionalization. As such, a primary objective of current research is to comparatively evaluate the dissolution relationship between polysaccharide structures and DES components, and to adapt DESs for specific applications. In this work, two typical galactomannans (LBG and GG), with same linear ẞ-1,4-linked D-mannose backbone but different M/G and molecular weight, were employed to study the effect of molecular weight and distribution pattern of Gal substituents on DESs dissolution. First, density functional theory (DFT) calculation was performed to predict the dissolution effects of GG and LBG fragment models in several traditional type II DESs. After preparing and characterizing a series of type II DESs, the optimal type II DES was screened from viscosity, polarity and solubility to LBG and GG. Subsequently, the dissolution mechanism of type II DESs on galactomannans was elucidated by DFT, molecular dynamics simulation (MD) and structural characterization of recovered polysaccharides. Taking advantage of DESs designability, type III DESs with AlCl3-6H2O as the third component were employed to achieve efficient dissolution of galactomannans. The effect of type III DESs with Lewis acid on the structure of the galactomannans during the solubilization was further evaluated by structural characterization of recovered galactomannans. This study aimed to explore the dissolution relationship between polysaccharides structure and DES components, to provide reference for the realization of DESs task specific functionalization and to fully utilize polysaccharide resources. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Choline chloride (ChCl), ethylene glycol (EG), urea, 1,4-butanediol (BDO), glycerin (GLY), potassium bromide (KBr), N,N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline (DMNA) and 4-nitroaniline (NA) were purchased from 2 D. Guo et al. Food Hydrocolloids 158 (2025) 110552 Jingchun Industry Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). In this study, all of the above reagents were of analytical grade. Guar bean gum (GG) and locust bean gum (LBG) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (USA) with the weight average molecular mass (Mw) of 2.25 x 10^6 g/mol and 8.65 x 10^5 g/mol, and polydispersity (PD) of 1.098 and 1.245, respectively. The monosaccharide composition of GG and LBG were D-mannose and D-galactose (M/G ratio of 1.20:1 and 3.63:1, respectively). ## 2.2. Computational methods Initial geometry optimizations of DESs and galactomannan model compounds were obtained using the B3LYP exchange-correlation function combined with the 6-311G (d, p) basis set (Pritchard, Altarawy, Didier, Gibson, & Windus, 2019; Stephens, Devlin, Chabalowski, & Frisch, 1994). To eliminate the dispersion effect, we added the key word of empirical dispersion = GD3BJ in the route section. Then, the initial structure of optimized DESs were performed at HF/6311G (d, p) level, and further reoptimized using the M06-2X exchange-correlation function in combination the 6-31++G (d, p) basis set based on the Gaussian 16 program package (Walker, Harvey, Sen, & Dessent, 2013). Given Gaussian results, the electrostatic surface potential (ESP) (Zhang & Lu, 2021), atom in molecules (AIM) (Bader, 1985), reduced density gradient (RDG) (Johnson et al., 2010) and frontline molecular orbitals (FMO) theory analyses were performed using the Multiwfn 3.8 programs (Lu & Chen, 2012). All the ESP, AIM and FMO maps were rendered by Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD) 1.9.4 program. The data of RDG was visualized by VMD 1.9.4 and Gnuplot 5.4.3 software. All molecular dynamics (MD) details were performed in Gromacs 2022.3, and all studied molecules were parameterized using the charm 36 force field (AitRaise et al., 2023; Xu, Kong, Peng, Wang, & Li, 2021). The (4M-1G)-C1E4 system consisted of 186 ChCl molecules, 744 EG molecules and one 4M-1G models molecular chain. The C1E4 compo- nents were added to a 6 nm × 6 nm × 6 nm box in a certain amount and proportion. Periodic boundary condition (PBC) was applied to the three directions of the box to ensure that the number of particles in the box was constant. Under certain temperature and pressure conditions, the steepest descent method was used to simulate the system in 50000 steps to minimize the energy of the system. Then the systems were equili- brated for 100 ps under NVT ensemble with temperature at 300 K. Following was a 100 ps simulation under NPT ensemble to equilibrate the solvents. Finally, a long-term MD simulation with a step size of 250 million steps and a duration of 500 ns was carried out at constant temperature and constant pressure. ### 2.3. Preparation of DESs First, all relevant materials were dried before preparation. Then, mixing HBAs with corresponding HBDs according to the molar ratio provided in Table S3 to prepare type II DESs. The mixture in the sealed bottle was stirred with a magnetic stirrer and heated at 80 °C until clear homogeneous liquid was obtained (Ramezani, Ahmadi, & Yamini, 2022). The preparation of *type III* DESs entailed weighing the corresponding components according to their composition and proportion, followed by stirring at 80 °C until a homogeneous and transparent liquid was formed. 2.4. Polarity determination of type II DESS Polarity scale (EN T), π* (dipolarity/polarizability), β (hydrogen bond basicity) and α (hydrogen bond acidity) values were calculated according to modified Kamlet-Taft empirical polarity scales (Ranjkesh, Parast, Strzeżysz, Zakerhamidi, & Yoon, 2018). 2.5. Measurement of viscosity The viscosity of the polysaccharide solution was measured using an Anton Paar Physica MCR 301 Rheometer (Anton Paar, GmbH, Austria) equipped with a cone-plate geometry (50 mm diameter). Samples were loaded onto a smooth Peltier plate which maintained constant experimental temperatures of 90 °C (±0.1 °C) for the studies presented herein. The plate spacing was 1 mm and temperature equilibration of the samples was achieved within 5 min prior to each measurement (Potier, Tea, Benyahia, Nicolai, & Renou, 2020). For each polysaccharide solution, steady shear and dynamic oscillatory shear experiments were carried out in the shear rate range of 0.1–1000 s⁻¹ and frequency range of 0.1–100 rad/s, respectively. All rheological data were analyzed with rheoplus software (Rheoplus/32 V3.40). ## 2.6. Solubility of galactomannans in different solvents The detailed measurement procedure for the solubility of galactomannans was based on the study by Cao et al. (Cao, Nian, Li, Wu, & Liu, 2019). Specifically, the dissolution process involved accurately weighing galactomannans (4 g ± 0.1 mg) into different solvents (60 mL ± 0.1 mL) and stirring the mixture magnetically at 80 °C for 5 h. The dissolved sample was centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 30 min, and the supernatant was collected. The supernatant was diluted 50 times with deionized water. Then, 1 mL of deionized water and 1 mL of 6% (w/v) phenol were added and mixed thoroughly. Next, 5 mL concentrated sulfuric acid was added to the mixture and fully mixed. After standing for 30 min, the absorption spectrum of the mixture at 490 nm was measured and calculated according to the following equation: $S = (A_{490nm}-b)/a \times 0.9 \times 10$ (1) Where $S$ represented the solubility of galactomannans (g/100 g), the absorbance of the mixture at 490 nm was expressed as $A_{490nm}$, the slope and intercept of the standard curve were expressed as $a$ and $b$. The standard curve was obtained by dissolving 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 g of glucose into 10 g of different DESs according to the above procedure. The determination process was performed in triplicate. The experimental data were analyzed using SPSS V.17.0 (p < 0.05). ## 2.7. Polarized light microscope 4 g GG and LBG were put into 60 mL different DESs, respectively, and stirred at 80 °C for 6–8 h. Dip a drop of GG solution onto a glass slide with a glass rod and observe it with a polarizing microscope (Axio scope A1, Carl Zeiss, Germany). 2.8. *Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy* The spectra were recorded at the wavenumber range of 4000–400 cm⁻¹ with FT-IR spectrophotometer (iS10, Thermo Nicolet, USA). The number of scans was 16 and referenced against air. The resolution of FT-IR was 4 cm⁻¹ (Beratto-Ramos, Agurto-Muñoz, Vargas-Montalba, & Castillo, 2020). 2.9. *NMR spectroscopy* ¹H and ¹H–¹H COSY NMR spectra were recorded at 25 °C by a Bruker Avance DPX-400 spectrometer (Bruker, Rheinstetten, Germany). Conclusion In this work, to elucidate how DES components affect the dissolution of polysaccharides with variable molecular weight and Gal substituent distribution, a systematic investigation was conducted using DFT calculation prediction, MD, and characterization of type II/III DESs and recovered galactomannans. Among the examined DESs, C1E4 with a high proportion of HBDs exhibited remarkable solubility by providing more H-bond sites. This result explained by the fact that C1E4 with a large number of anionic and neutral H-bonds broke the original galactomannan H-bond networks and rebuilt new hydrogen bonds. The solubility of galactomannans was related to its molecular weight and distribution pattern of Gal substituents, which could be explained that the repulsive interactions hindered H-bonds breaking due to the high molecular weight and rich Gal side-chains ("hairy" regions) for GG, resulting low solubility (0.16 g/100 mL). Additionally, it was indicated that immense number of active acid sites in type III DESs not only effectively broke and rebuilt the galactomannans H-bond networks, but also cleaved the glycosidic bond to obtain recovered polysaccharides with target molecular weight. Taken together, this work provided a promising strategy for development of task specific DESs and their widespread polysaccharide resources application in the future.
